title: Strategic reminder setting for time-based intentions: Influence of metacognition, delay length, and cue visibility
research_question: How do delay length, metacognitive beliefs, and access to a visible time cue influence strategic reminder setting and performance for time-based prospective-memory intentions?
methodology: Experiment 1 used a preregistered within-subject 3-by-2 design with 52 Prolific participants, manipulating 10-, 20-, and 30-second delays and unaided versus reminder conditions while participants concurrently performed a two-back task with a visible clock. Experiment 2 used a preregistered 3-by-2-by-2 design with a final sample of 96 participants, adding a between-subject manipulation in which the clock was either continuously visible or had to be deliberately revealed. Participants made prospective and retrospective confidence judgements, and the authors analysed prospective-memory accuracy, false alarms, misses, reminder use, clock checking, metacognitive bias, and ongoing-task performance using ANOVA, correlations, and regression models in R.

key_findings.finding: Longer delays reduced first-response prospective-memory accuracy, lowered confidence, and substantially increased reminder use.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 Results: Effect of delay length

key_findings.finding: Setting reminders improved prospective-memory performance, reduced errors, and produced larger benefits at longer delays in both experiments.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 PM performance improvement; Experiment 2 PM performance improvement

key_findings.finding: Within participants, a steeper decline in confidence as delay increased predicted a steeper rise in reminder use, even though the confidence decline did not track the corresponding decline in objective unaided accuracy.
key_findings.section: Experiment 1 Metacognitive judgement and reminder usage; General Discussion

key_findings.finding: The preregistered hypothesis that people with lower average confidence across participants would generally use more reminders was not consistently supported; mean confidence did not significantly predict overall reminder use in the main analyses.
key_findings.section: Experiments 1 and 2: Metacognitive judgement and reminder usage

key_findings.finding: Participants used significantly more reminders when the clock was hidden than when it remained visible, and clock visibility explained reminder usage independently of average confidence in Experiment 2.
key_findings.section: Experiment 2 Reminder usage and General Discussion

key_findings.finding: Unaided prospective-memory accuracy did not significantly differ between visible- and hidden-clock groups, but hiding the clock imposed a measurable cost on the concurrent two-back task.
key_findings.section: Experiment 2 PM performance and General Discussion: Time monitoring behaviour

key_findings.finding: Among hidden-clock participants, more frequent deliberate clock checking was associated with better unaided prospective-memory accuracy.
Objective performance differences did not reliably drive reminder allocation across delay conditions, indicating that strategic offloading followed perceived need more closely than measured need.

limitations: The maximum intention delay was only 30 seconds, whereas many everyday and workplace intentions persist for minutes, hours, or days.
Participants were instructed to prioritize the ongoing two-back task, and reminder strategies might differ when the prospective task has higher priority.
The controlled online task does not establish that the same reminder-allocation behavior occurs in naturalistic workplace environments.
Experiment 2 excluded participants who never used reminders, which narrows conclusions about population-level differences in reminder propensity.
Several informative analyses were exploratory or non-preregistered and therefore require greater caution than the primary preregistered tests.
The study addresses individual time-based intentions rather than explicit longitudinal work-item state transitions, cross-thread aggregation, or omission/repetition in briefings.
raw_claims: Experiment 1 compared 10-, 20-, and 30-second intentions under unaided and reminder conditions.
Experiment 2 additionally compared a continuously visible clock with a clock that participants had to reveal manually.
Participants became less confident as intention delays increased.
Reminder use increased as delays became longer.
External reminders improved prospective-memory accuracy and reduced errors.
The reminder benefit was generally larger at longer delays.
The within-person change in confidence across delays predicted the within-person change in reminder use.
Average confidence across individuals did not consistently predict how many reminders they used.
Participants used more reminders when the clock was hidden.
Hiding the clock did not significantly reduce unaided prospective-memory accuracy but increased demands on the concurrent task.
More frequent clock checking in the hidden-clock condition was associated with better unaided prospective-memory performance.
The experiments and analysis plans were preregistered.
Data and analysis code for both experiments were made available through OSF.
